findings.message: The fix removes any redirect with any target, not just `&>`. Together with the new `cat`, `grep` and `sort` entries in ALLOWED, a call that overwrites an arbitrary file now passes in block mode. That contradicts the documented rule that block denies everything except commit, `cd`, read-only filters and the hand-off. The strip should only remove fd duplication (`N>&M`) and redirects to /dev/null or to a file under the `.specclaw` hand-off path. Any other file target should leave the redirect in place so the call is denied. Write redirects (`>` and `>>` to a real file) should also be tested as deny rows.
findings.scenario: At the cap in block mode, Bash `git log | cat > src/app.py` (or `grep x a.txt > src/app.py`). The strip turns `> src/app.py` into a space. Parts become `git log` and `cat`, both match ALLOWED, so `committing()` returns True and the call exits 0. The agent has written a source file after being told to stop, where the gate should deny it.

findings.message: The new regex handles `>`, `>>` and `<` with spaced and unspaced targets, fd-prefixed forms such as `1>f` and `2>>f`, and input redirects. The table only exercises `2>&1`, `/dev/null`, `>&2`, `&>` and `&>>`. Add pass rows for `git log < in`, `git status 1>out` and `git log 2>> e`. Add a deny row such as `git log > f; rm x`.
findings.scenario: Rewrite the strip so `<` or a spaced `> target` is no longer removed. Every row in the table stays green, so a regression in those forms goes unnoticed.
